1.title: What is the difference between value types and reference types in C#?
1.answer:
Value types hold the data DIRECTLY on the stack and are copied by value. When you assign one int to another, you get an independent copy.

Reference types hold a POINTER on the stack — the actual object lives on the heap. When you assign a class instance to another variable, both variables point to the SAME object on the heap.
1.keyPoints: Stack (value) vs Heap (reference) | int / float / bool / struct / enum = value | class / string / array / interface = reference | null only valid for reference types

2.title: Difference between String and StringBuilder
2.answer:
String is IMMUTABLE — every modification creates a brand-new string object on the heap. The old one is left for the garbage collector. Fine for a few ops, expensive in loops.

StringBuilder is MUTABLE — it owns a resizable internal char buffer. Appends modify the SAME instance without creating new objects.
2.keyPoints: Immutable vs Mutable | String = GC pressure in loops | StringBuilder = loops, big text, CSV/HTML builders | Rule: < 5 concats use String, more use StringBuilder

3.title: What is the difference between ref, out, and in parameters?
3.answer:
ref — must be initialized before the call. The method can READ and WRITE.
out — does NOT need initialization. The method MUST assign a value before returning. Used to return multiple values.
in — passed by reference, but READ-ONLY. Used for performance when passing big structs.
3.keyPoints: ref = read+write, must init | out = write contract, no init | in = readonly reference, perf for large structs

4.title: What is async / await? How does it actually work?
4.answer:
async/await lets you write non-blocking I/O code that LOOKS synchronous.

When you await a Task, the runtime:
1. Starts the operation (DB call, HTTP request, file I/O).
2. RELEASES the current thread back to the thread pool — the thread is free to handle other requests.
3. When the operation completes, a continuation runs and your method resumes from the await line.

The compiler rewrites your async method into a state machine. That's how one ASP.NET server can handle thousands of concurrent users.
4.keyPoints: Non-blocking I/O | Returns Task / Task<T> / ValueTask | NEVER use .Result or .Wait() — deadlocks | Async all the way down | async void only for event handlers

5.title: What are delegates, Func, Action and Predicate?
5.answer:
A delegate is a TYPE-SAFE pointer to a method. It lets you treat a method as a first-class value — pass it as a parameter, store it in a field, invoke it later.

Built-in shortcuts:
• Func<T1,...,TResult> — a method that RETURNS something.
• Action<T1,...> — a method that returns VOID.
• Predicate<T> — a method that returns BOOL (shorthand for Func<T,bool>).
5.keyPoints: Method pointers | Backbone of LINQ, events, callbacks | Lambdas (x => x*2) compile to delegates | Multicast: += / -=

6.title: What is LINQ? Deferred vs immediate execution
6.answer:
LINQ (Language INtegrated Query) gives a uniform query syntax for collections, databases, XML, JSON.

Deferred — Where / Select / OrderBy DO NOT run when written. The query only executes when you enumerate (foreach, ToList, First, Count, Sum). Re-enumerating runs it again — surprise re-queries!

Immediate — ToList(), ToArray(), Count(), Sum(), First() run the query immediately and materialize the result.
6.keyPoints: IEnumerable<T> = LINQ-to-Objects | IQueryable<T> = translates to SQL via EF | Deferred = composable, lazy | Immediate = run-now, materialize | Call ToList() to lock in results
6.codeSnippet:
var young = users.Where(u => u.Age < 30);   // query built, NOT run

foreach (var u in young) { ... }            // runs once here

var list = young.ToList();                  // runs AGAIN
int count = young.Count();                  // runs AGAIN

7.title: Difference between .NET Framework, .NET Core and .NET 5+ (just "NET")
7.answer:
.NET Framework (last v4.8) — Windows-only, the original .NET. Used by legacy enterprise apps. No more new features.
.NET Core (1.0 → 3.1) — Microsoft's open-source, cross-platform rewrite. Faster, modular, runs on Windows / Linux / macOS.
.NET 5+ (5, 6, 7, 8, 9) — "Core" was dropped. One unified .NET for web, desktop, mobile (MAUI), cloud, IoT. .NET 8 and 9 are what you use for any new project today.
7.keyPoints: Framework = Windows-only, legacy | Core = deprecated name | .NET 8 (LTS) / 9 (Current) = what to learn | Same SDK installs all workloads

8.title: Explain the ASP.NET Core middleware pipeline
8.answer:
Every request flows through a CHAIN of middleware components. Each one can:
  1. Inspect / modify the request.
  2. Call await next() to pass control on.
  3. Inspect / modify the response on the way back.

The ORDER you register middleware matters. Standard order: ExceptionHandler → HTTPS → Static files → Routing → CORS → Authentication → Authorization → Endpoints.
8.keyPoints: Chain of responsibility | Order = critical | UseAuthentication BEFORE UseAuthorization | Terminal middleware (MapControllers) doesn't call next

9.title: What are the three Dependency Injection lifetimes?
9.answer:
ASP.NET Core has a built-in DI container with three lifetimes:

• Transient — a NEW instance every time it is requested. Use for lightweight, stateless services.
• Scoped — ONE instance per HTTP request. Same instance shared throughout that request. Use for DbContext, per-request state.
• Singleton — ONE instance for the entire application lifetime. Use for stateless config, caches, HttpClient factory. Must be thread-safe.
9.keyPoints: Transient = always new | Scoped = once per request | Singleton = once per app | Never inject Scoped into Singleton (captive dependency bug)

10.title: IActionResult vs ActionResult<T>
10.answer:
IActionResult — flexible return type (Ok, NotFound, BadRequest, File, Redirect…) but you LOSE compile-time info about your data shape.
ActionResult<T> — generic. Lets you return EITHER a status helper (NotFound(), BadRequest()) OR a concrete T directly. The response shape becomes self-documenting in Swagger.
10.keyPoints: Prefer ActionResult<T> in new APIs | Implicit conversion from T and from ActionResult | Combine with [ProducesResponseType] for OpenAPI

11.title: What is CORS and how to configure it in ASP.NET Core?
11.answer:
CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a BROWSER security feature. By default, JavaScript on https://site-A.com is blocked from calling https://api-B.com.

The API must respond with Access-Control-Allow-Origin / Methods / Headers to tell the browser "this origin is allowed." In ASP.NET Core you do this with a CORS policy + app.UseCors().
11.keyPoints: Browser-enforced — not a server firewall | Must be added BEFORE UseAuthorization | AllowAnyOrigin + AllowCredentials are NOT allowed together

12.title: What is JWT authentication? How does it work in ASP.NET Core?
12.answer:
JWT (JSON Web Token) is a self-contained, signed string used for stateless authentication.

Flow:
  1. User POSTs username + password to /login.
  2. Server validates credentials → builds JWT with claims (userId, role, exp) → signs with a secret key.
  3. Server returns the token to the client.
  4. Client stores it (localStorage / httpOnly cookie) and sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>` on every request.
  5. Server verifies the signature and expiry. NO database lookup needed — claims live inside the token.
12.keyPoints: Stateless = no session storage | 3 parts: header.payload.signature (base64) | NEVER store passwords / PII in payload | Short expiry (15m) + refresh tokens

13.title: What are the 4 pillars of OOP? Explain with code.
13.answer:
1. ENCAPSULATION — bundle data + methods together; hide internal state behind properties.
2. INHERITANCE — a class reuses members of another class.
3. POLYMORPHISM — one interface, many concrete forms (virtual / override + overloading).
4. ABSTRACTION — expose WHAT a class does, hide HOW it does it.
13.keyPoints: E.I.P.A. | Encapsulation hides DATA | Abstraction hides DETAIL | Polymorphism = virtual/override and overloading

14.title: Abstract class vs Interface — when do you use which?
14.answer:
Abstract class — partial implementation. Has fields, constructors, implemented + abstract methods. A class can inherit ONLY ONE. Use when you want shared base behavior.
Interface — pure contract: WHAT a type can do. No fields. A class can implement MANY. Use to define capabilities (IDisposable, IComparable, IUserService).

Rule of thumb: IS-A → abstract class. CAN-DO → interface.

15.title: What are SOLID principles?
15.answer:
S — Single Responsibility: a class should have ONE reason to change.
O — Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification. Add new behavior by new classes, not by editing existing ones.
L — Liskov Substitution: a subclass must be usable wherever its parent is used, without surprises.
I — Interface Segregation: many small, focused interfaces beat one fat one.
D — Dependency Inversion: depend on ABSTRACTIONS, not concretions. (DI containers solve this.)
15.keyPoints: S.O.L.I.D. | DI in ASP.NET Core IS the D | Most real refactors fix S and D | Skinny interfaces beat fat ones

16.title: What are components and what is a standalone component?
16.answer:
A component = TypeScript class + @Component decorator pairing a template, styles, and logic. The basic building block.

Standalone components (Angular 14+) do NOT need NgModule. They import their dependencies directly via `imports: [...]` on @Component. From Angular 17+ this is the default; from 20+ apps typically have NO NgModules at all.
16.keyPoints: Class + decorator + template + styles | standalone: true | imports: [CommonModule, FormsModule] | bootstrapApplication() in main.ts

17.title: What is data binding? Explain all four types.
17.answer:
1. Interpolation — {{ value }} → one-way, class to template, used inside text.
2. Property binding — [src]="imgUrl" → one-way, class to DOM property.
3. Event binding — (click)="save()" → one-way, template to class, on DOM events.
4. Two-way binding — [(ngModel)]="name" → property + event combined. Needs FormsModule.

18.title: Observable vs Promise
18.answer:
Promise — single, eager value, NOT cancellable. Calling .then runs immediately. Good for one-shot async ops.
Observable (RxJS) — a STREAM that can emit multiple values over time, LAZY (subscribing starts it), CANCELLABLE (unsubscribe stops it), with rich operators (map, filter, debounceTime, switchMap, retry). Angular's HttpClient returns Observables.
18.keyPoints: Single vs stream | Eager vs lazy | Cancellable via unsubscribe | takeUntilDestroyed / async pipe to auto-cleanup

19.title: What are Angular Signals?
19.answer:
Signals are Angular's reactivity primitive (stable in v17+). A signal holds a value AND notifies anyone depending on it when the value changes.

Types:
• signal(value) — writable.
• computed(() => …) — derived; auto-recomputes.
• effect(() => …) — side-effect runs when its signals change.

Why: more predictable than Zone.js change detection, fewer unnecessary re-renders, foundation of Angular's zoneless future. Templates auto-track signal reads — no .subscribe needed.
19.keyPoints: signal / computed / effect | Read with mySignal(), write with .set() / .update() | Zoneless-friendly | RxJS bridge: toSignal / toObservable

20.title: Template-driven vs Reactive forms
20.answer:
Template-driven — form structure lives in HTML via ngModel. Angular builds the FormGroup behind the scenes. Easy for small forms.
Reactive — form defined in TypeScript as FormGroup of FormControls. Validation, dynamic fields, conditional logic, unit tests — all easier. Preferred for any non-trivial form.

21.title: What is Lazy Loading and how do you implement it?
21.answer:
Lazy loading splits the bundle so a feature's code is downloaded ONLY when the user navigates there. Massive drop in initial load time.

In Angular 17+ standalone: use `loadComponent` for one route, `loadChildren` for a route subtree.
21.keyPoints: Per-route code splitting | loadComponent vs loadChildren | Combine with preloading strategy for UX | Visible in Network tab as separate chunks

22.title: var vs let vs const — what's the real difference?
22.answer:
var — function-scoped, hoisted (initialized to undefined), can be re-declared. Legacy.
let — block-scoped, hoisted but in temporal dead zone until declared, can be re-assigned but not re-declared in the same scope.
const — block-scoped, cannot be re-assigned. Object/array CONTENTS can still change — the binding is fixed, not the value.
22.keyPoints: Function vs block scope | TDZ for let/const | const binding ≠ deep immutability | Default to const, switch to let only when needed

23.title: Difference between == and === in JavaScript
23.answer:
== performs type coercion before comparing. Full of surprises and bugs.
=== compares value AND type. Always prefer ===.
23.keyPoints: Loose vs strict equality | TypeScript / ESLint warns on == | Use === unless you specifically need the null-undefined trick
23.codeSnippet:
0   == ''         // true  😱
0   === ''        // false

null == undefined // true  (the ONE useful coercion)
null === undefined// false

'5' == 5          // true
'5' === 5         // false

24.title: Explain closures in JavaScript with an example
24.answer:
A closure is a function that REMEMBERS variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope finishes. This is how JS implements private state, factory functions, and callbacks.

The inner function holds a LIVE reference to outer variables — not a copy.
24.keyPoints: Inner function + outer variables | Private state pattern | Loop var capture bug in old `var` code — fixed with `let`

25.title: TypeScript interface vs type
25.answer:
Both describe the shape of a value. Differences:
• interface can be RE-OPENED (declaration merging).
• type is a fixed alias — cannot be merged.
• type can describe primitives, unions, intersections, tuples — interface cannot.
• Both can be extended (extends / &).

Rule of thumb: `interface` for object shapes that may evolve; `type` for unions, primitives, and computed types.
25.keyPoints: Declaration merging — only interface | Unions / primitives — only type | Interchangeable for plain object shapes

26.title: INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL — what is the difference?
26.answer:
INNER JOIN — rows where the ON condition matches in BOTH tables.
LEFT JOIN — ALL rows from the left + matches from right (NULL where no match).
RIGHT JOIN — mirror of LEFT.
FULL JOIN — rows from both, NULL where unmatched.
CROSS JOIN — Cartesian product (rare).
26.keyPoints: Venn diagrams help | LEFT JOIN + WHERE right.col IS NULL = anti-join | Real queries are usually INNER or LEFT
26.codeSnippet:
-- All customers, with their orders if any (NULL otherwise)
SELECT c.Name, o.OrderId, o.Total
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.CustomerId = c.Id
ORDER BY c.Name;
26.commonUsage:
-- Anti-join: customers who never placed an order
SELECT c.Id, c.Name
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.CustomerId = c.Id
WHERE o.OrderId IS NULL;

-- Multi-table inner join
SELECT u.Name, p.Title, c.Name AS Category
FROM Posts p
INNER JOIN Users u      ON u.Id = p.AuthorId
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.Id = p.CategoryId
WHERE p.PublishedAt IS NOT NULL;

27.title: WHERE vs HAVING
27.answer:
WHERE filters rows BEFORE grouping (row-level).
HAVING filters AFTER GROUP BY (group-level). Used with aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN).

Aggregates are NOT allowed in WHERE — they are only computed after grouping.
27.keyPoints: WHERE = before group | HAVING = after group | Aggregates only in HAVING (or SELECT/ORDER BY)
27.codeSnippet:
-- Customers who placed > 5 orders in 2026
SELECT CustomerId, COUNT(*) AS OrderCount
FROM Orders
WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-01-01'    -- filter rows first
GROUP BY CustomerId
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;                -- filter groups
27.commonUsage:
-- Top categories by revenue
SELECT c.Name, SUM(oi.Quantity * oi.Price) AS Revenue
FROM OrderItems oi
INNER JOIN Products p   ON p.Id = oi.ProductId
INNER JOIN Categories c ON c.Id = p.CategoryId
WHERE oi.CreatedAt >= '2026-01-01'
GROUP BY c.Name
HAVING SUM(oi.Quantity * oi.Price) > 100000
ORDER BY Revenue DESC;

28.title: Stored procedures — what are they and why use them?
28.answer:
A stored procedure is a precompiled set of SQL statements stored in the database under a name. Call it from the app via EXEC.

Advantages:
• Performance — cached execution plan.
• Security — grant EXEC only; no direct table access; parameterized = SQL-injection safe.
• Maintainability — change SQL in one place, no app redeploy.
• Less network chatter — one round trip per call.
28.keyPoints: Precompiled + cached | Parameterized = safe | EXEC vs sp_executesql | Combine with EF via FromSqlRaw / SqlQuery

29.title: Index — Clustered vs Non-clustered
29.answer:
An index is a data structure (B-tree) that lets the DB find rows fast without scanning the whole table.

Clustered — defines the PHYSICAL order of rows. ONE per table. The PK is clustered by default. Leaf level IS the table.
Non-clustered — separate structure with key columns + pointer to the row. MANY per table.

Trade-off: indexes speed SELECT but slow INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
29.keyPoints: One clustered, many non-clustered | Don't over-index | INCLUDE columns = covering index | Watch fragmentation
29.codeSnippet:
-- Clustered (typically on PK, automatic)
CREATE CLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_OrderDate
ON Orders (OrderDate);

-- Non-clustered with included columns (covering)
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Orders_Customer
ON Orders (CustomerId)
INCLUDE (OrderDate, Total);
29.commonUsage:
-- Find slow queries that would benefit from indexes
SELECT TOP 20
    qs.execution_count,
    qs.total_logical_reads / qs.execution_count AS AvgReads,
    SUBSTRING(qt.text, qs.statement_start_offset/2 + 1, 200) AS Query
FROM sys.dm_exec_query_stats qs
CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(qs.sql_handle) qt
ORDER BY AvgReads DESC;

30.title: CTE and Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, PARTITION BY)
30.answer:
CTE — a named temporary result set defined with WITH. Improves readability over nested subqueries; supports recursion.
Window functions — compute across a 'window' of rows WITHOUT collapsing them. ROW_NUMBER assigns sequence; RANK leaves gaps for ties; DENSE_RANK does not. PARTITION BY restarts the calculation per group.
30.keyPoints: WITH cte AS (…) | func OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …) | Recursive CTE for trees/hierarchies
30.codeSnippet:
-- Latest order per customer
WITH Ranked AS (
    SELECT o.*,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER
             (PARTITION BY o.CustomerId ORDER BY o.OrderDate DESC) AS rn
    FROM Orders o
)
SELECT *
FROM Ranked
WHERE rn = 1;
30.commonUsage:
-- Recursive CTE — get a manager's full org tree
WITH OrgTree AS (
    SELECT Id, Name, ManagerId, 0 AS Level
    FROM Employees
    WHERE ManagerId IS NULL                -- root

    UNION ALL

    SELECT e.Id, e.Name, e.ManagerId, t.Level + 1
    FROM Employees e
    INNER JOIN OrgTree t ON e.ManagerId = t.Id
)
SELECT * FROM OrgTree ORDER BY Level, Name;

31.title: Code-First vs Database-First in EF Core
31.answer:
Code-First — you write C# entity classes + DbContext; EF generates SQL migrations to create/update the DB. Best for greenfield, fully version-controlled with code.
Database-First — you have an existing DB; you scaffold entity classes from it. Good for legacy DBs.

    "Server=.;Database=Shop;Trusted_Connection=true" \

32.title: Eager vs Lazy vs Explicit loading
32.answer:
Eager — load related data UPFRONT with .Include(). One query with JOINs.
Lazy — related data is loaded ON FIRST ACCESS of a nav property. Needs `virtual` + Proxies package. Convenient but N+1 trap.
Explicit — call _db.Entry(entity).Reference(...).Load() manually.

Prefer eager by default; lazy is convenient but a performance landmine.
32.keyPoints: .Include() / .ThenInclude() | N+1 problem | AsSplitQuery() for big Includes | AsNoTracking() for read-only
32.codeSnippet:
// Eager loading with multiple levels
var orders = await _db.Orders
    .Include(o => o.Customer)
    .Include(o => o.Items)
        .ThenInclude(i => i.Product)
    .AsNoTracking()
    .ToListAsync();

33.title: The N+1 problem — what is it and how to fix it
33.answer:
N+1 happens when you load N parent rows with one query, then access a nav property in a loop — triggering N additional queries. Total: N+1 round trips.

Looks fine in dev with 5 rows. Crushes performance in prod with 5000.

Fix: eager-load via .Include() or use a projection (.Select).
33.keyPoints: Watch for nav property access inside foreach | Enable EF logging in dev | Projection (Select) often beats Include for read-only DTOs

34.title: HTTP verbs — when to use each
34.answer:
GET — read data. Safe (no side effects) and idempotent. Can be cached.
POST — create OR non-idempotent action. Has body. Not idempotent.
PUT — replace a resource fully. Idempotent.
PATCH — partial update. Idempotent if done right.
DELETE — remove a resource. Idempotent.

35.title: REST vs SOAP
35.answer:
REST — architectural style over HTTP. Lightweight JSON, stateless, easy to consume from any client. Default for modern web/mobile APIs.
SOAP — protocol using XML, strict contracts (WSDL), built-in WS-* standards for security / transactions. Heavier. Used in some banking / B2B integrations.
Rule of thumb: build REST unless you specifically need WS-* features. gRPC is the modern high-perf alternative for service-to-service.
35.keyPoints: REST = JSON, stateless, simple | SOAP = XML, contract, enterprise | gRPC = binary, fast, internal services

36.title: Authentication vs Authorization
36.answer:
Authentication — WHO are you? Verifying identity (username/password, JWT, OAuth, Windows auth).
Authorization — WHAT are you allowed to do? Checking permissions / roles / policies AFTER we know who you are.
UseAuthentication() must come BEFORE UseAuthorization() in Program.cs.
36.keyPoints: AuthN = identity | AuthZ = permissions | UseAuthentication BEFORE UseAuthorization | Role-based, policy-based, claims-based

37.title: Generic try-catch with structured logging (controller pattern)
37.answer: Every public action should have a defensive try-catch ONLY if you need to convert a specific exception into a domain response. For everything else, lean on an exception middleware. This is the bog-standard pattern you copy 10 times a week.
37.keyPoints: Don't swallow exceptions silently | Always log with context | Return ProblemDetails or a clean message | Prefer global middleware over per-action try-catch

38.title: Repository + Service pattern with DI
38.answer: Standard layering: Controller → Service (business rules) → Repository (data access). Everything depends on interfaces; the DI container wires it up. This is what every clean-architecture codebase looks like.
38.keyPoints: Controller is thin — no business logic | Service has rules | Repository has DB queries only | Register lifetimes in Program.cs

39.title: Pagination with EF Core
39.answer: Every list endpoint should be paged. Standard pattern: page + pageSize from query string, Skip/Take in EF, return items + total count.
39.keyPoints: Always cap pageSize (e.g., max 100) | Return totalCount for paging UI | Use AsNoTracking for read-only lists

40.title: File upload (multipart/form-data) in ASP.NET Core

51.title: What's your current and expected CTC?
51.answer:
This question filters candidates by cost — and it can either anchor you low or set the stage for a strong number.

3. Justify the range with: years of experience, similar role market rate (LinkedIn / AmbitionBox / Glassdoor), the JD's seniority.
4. Anchor on TOTAL CTC (fixed + variable + ESOPs + joining bonus + relocation), not just fixed.

52.title: How do you handle a counter-offer from your current company?
52.answer:
Most counter-offers are RETENTION tactics — your manager doesn't want the workload of finding a replacement. Industry data: 80% of people who accept a counter-offer leave within 12 months anyway.

FRAMEWORK:
1. Acknowledge the new offer respectfully — never use it as leverage.
2. Map your REAL reasons for leaving (growth, tech, role, manager, comp). If they're addressable with money alone, the counter may work. If they're structural (no growth path, dead tech), money won't fix it.
3. If the new offer's gap is large and the reasons are solid → take it. Counter-offers rarely close growth-driven moves.
52.keyPoints: Most counters fail in 12 months | Money is rarely the real reason you're leaving | Be transparent with the new employer if you're still considering | Don't leverage the counter to squeeze the new offer
52.commonUsage:
// What to say when current company counter-offers

"I really appreciate the counter — it means a lot.
 Honestly, my reasons for moving aren't just compensation,
 they're <specific reason: scope / domain / tech>.

 I've already given my word to <new company>. Switching back now
 wouldn't be fair to them or to me."

// What NOT to do: shop the counter back to the new company.

53.title: Design a URL shortener (like bit.ly)
53.answer:
REQUIREMENTS
• Functional: take a long URL → return a short slug (e.g., bit.ly/abc123). Hit the slug → redirect.
• Non-functional: read-heavy (~100:1), low latency on redirect, 6-year retention.

KEY DESIGN CHOICES

1. ID generation
   • Option A — counter + base62 encode (1 → '1', 62 → '10', etc.). 7 chars = 3.5T URLs.
   • Option B — hash the long URL (MD5/SHA), take first 7 chars, handle collisions.
   Counter+base62 wins for predictability and no collision logic.

2. Storage
   • Single table: slug (PK), long_url, created_at, expires_at, user_id.
   • Reads dominate — slap a Redis cache in front (>95% hit rate).

3. Read path
   GET /:slug → Redis → if miss → SQL → cache it → 301 redirect.

4. Write path
   POST /shorten → get next ID from a distributed counter (ZooKeeper / DB sequence) → base62 → store → return.

5. Scale
   • Reads — add cache + read replicas.
   • Writes — shard counter by ID range; multiple write nodes each handle a range.
   • Analytics — fire 'click' events to Kafka, aggregate offline.
53.keyPoints: Base62 encoding | Read-heavy ⇒ aggressive caching | Distributed counter > hashing | 301 (permanent) redirect to leverage browser cache | Soft delete for expiry, not hard delete
53.followUps: How do you handle custom slugs? | What if two users want the same custom slug at the same time? | How do you support analytics (clicks per hour, geo)? | What if a shortened URL is abused for phishing — how do you take it down?
53.antiPatterns: Using GUIDs as slugs — too long for users | Hot-keyed cache (one viral link) — protect with rate limiting at edge | Storing click events synchronously in the redirect path — kills latency | 302 instead of 301 — browsers don't cache, every visit hits your server

54.title: SQL vs NoSQL — when do you choose which?
54.answer:
SQL (relational — Postgres, SQL Server, MySQL)
• Strong schema, ACID transactions, joins, mature tooling.
• Best when: data has clear structure, relationships matter, consistency is critical (banking, orders, inventory).

NoSQL families
• Document (Mongo, CosmosDB) — flexible JSON; great for user profiles, product catalogs.
• Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB) — O(1) lookup; sessions, caches, leaderboards.
• Wide-column (Cassandra) — huge write throughput; time-series, telemetry.
• Graph (Neo4j) — relationship-heavy domains; social networks, fraud, recommendations.

RULE OF THUMB
• Default to SQL — you can always denormalize. Going the other way is hard.
• Reach for NoSQL when you have ONE clear access pattern at huge scale, OR when the data is genuinely schema-less.
54.keyPoints: Default to SQL | NoSQL is per-access-pattern, not per-company | ACID vs BASE | Eventual consistency = harder to reason about | Polyglot persistence is normal in real systems
54.videoSearchQuery: sql vs nosql when to use system design
54.followUps: What is CAP theorem and which corner does each DB pick? | Explain eventual consistency with a real example | How does Mongo's transaction support compare to Postgres? | What is a denormalized read model and when do you build one?
54.antiPatterns: Picking MongoDB because 'we move fast' — pain hits at month 6 when relations grow | Putting financial data in a BASE store | Doing N joins client-side because 'we wanted NoSQL' | Using SQL with a row-per-event schema instead of a real time-series DB

55.title: Cache-aside, write-through, write-behind — explain each
55.answer:
CACHE-ASIDE (most common, simplest)
• App reads cache → on miss, reads DB → writes back to cache.
• App writes DB → INVALIDATES cache.
• Pros: simple, app fully in control. Cons: stale reads on race conditions.

WRITE-THROUGH
• App writes to cache; cache synchronously writes to DB.
• Pros: cache always fresh. Cons: every write pays cache + DB latency.

WRITE-BEHIND (write-back)
• App writes to cache; cache asynchronously flushes to DB later.
• Pros: super-fast writes. Cons: data loss risk if cache crashes; complex to operate.
55.keyPoints: Cache-aside is the 90% default | Write-through for read-heavy + low-staleness tolerance | Write-behind for write-heavy + can tolerate small loss | TTL + cache stampede protection both matter
55.videoSearchQuery: caching strategies cache aside write through write behind
55.followUps: What is a thundering herd / cache stampede? | How do you prevent it (lock, refresh-ahead, request coalescing)? | What is TTL jitter and why use it? | How do you bust cache across multiple app instances?
55.antiPatterns: Forgetting to invalidate on write — stale data | TTL too long → stale; too short → useless | One huge key that all requests hit — single point of contention | Storing the result of a join — invalidation becomes a nightmare

56.title: Sessions vs JWT — which should you use for auth?
56.answer:
SESSIONS (cookie + server store)
• Server creates a session ID, sets it as an httpOnly cookie, looks it up in Redis on every request.
• Pros: revocation is instant (delete the session row), opaque to client, small cookie.
• Cons: requires server-side store, sticky sessions or distributed store across nodes.

JWT (signed token)
• Server signs a token with claims, client sends it on every request, server only verifies signature + expiry.
• Pros: stateless — scales horizontally, works great for microservices.
• Cons: hard to revoke before expiry — need a blacklist or short TTL + refresh tokens.

MODERN PICK
• Browser-only app: sessions in httpOnly cookies — easier and safer (XSS-resistant).
• Mobile + multi-service backend: JWT with refresh tokens.
56.keyPoints: Sessions = stateful, easy revocation | JWT = stateless, fast scale-out, harder revocation | httpOnly + sameSite cookies guard XSS / CSRF | Short access token + refresh token is the sweet spot
56.videoSearchQuery: sessions vs jwt authentication system design
56.followUps: How would you implement 'log out everywhere'? | What is a refresh-token rotation? | What is the OAuth 2.0 PKCE flow? | How do you protect a JWT-protected SPA from CSRF?
56.antiPatterns: Long-lived JWTs (days/weeks) with no revocation strategy | Storing JWTs in localStorage in XSS-exposed apps | Using sessions but sharing them across services with HTTP calls | Putting all claims in the JWT — token bloat at every request

57.title: Monolith vs Microservices — when to choose which
57.answer:
MONOLITH
• One deployable, one DB. Simple to develop, test, deploy.
• Wins early-stage and for small teams. 80% of products NEVER outgrow it.
• Modular monolith = clear boundaries within the codebase, single deployment.

MICROSERVICES
• Many independently deployable services, each owning its data store.
• Wins at SCALE — independent teams, independent release cadence, polyglot tech.
• Cost: distributed systems complexity (network, retries, saga, idempotency, tracing, ops).

RULE
• Start with a monolith. Extract services ONLY when team/scale pain forces it.
• If you have < 10 engineers, you almost certainly should not be doing microservices.
57.keyPoints: Default to modular monolith | Microservices = organizational scaling tool first, perf second | Conway's Law — services mirror team structure | Distributed tx are HARD (Saga, outbox)
57.videoSearchQuery: monolith vs microservices when to use
57.followUps: What is the Saga pattern? | How do you handle distributed transactions across services? | What is the Outbox pattern for reliable messaging? | What is service mesh and when do you need one?
57.antiPatterns: Microservices that share a database — defeats the purpose | Distributed monolith (services that all deploy together) | Premature extraction — pain of distributed system without benefit | Skipping observability (tracing, correlation IDs) — you'll regret it on day 2

58.title: Load balancer vs API gateway — what's the difference?
58.answer:
LOAD BALANCER (L4 / L7)
• Distributes traffic across many instances of the SAME service.
• L4 (NLB) = TCP-level routing.
• L7 (ALB / nginx) = HTTP-aware — host, path, headers.
• Concerned with availability + spreading load.

API GATEWAY
• Single entry point for MANY services. Does:
  - Routing per path (/users → user-svc, /orders → order-svc).
  - Auth (JWT / OAuth) once at the edge.
  - Rate limiting, throttling, quotas.
  - Request / response shaping, aggregation, versioning.
  - Metrics, observability.

IN PRACTICE
• Behind the LB you may have N gateway instances. Behind the gateway, each backend has its own LB. Both layers exist.
58.keyPoints: LB = spread traffic within one service | Gateway = route + auth + policy across many services | Examples: nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB · Kong, Ocelot, YARP, AWS API Gateway | Both can do health checks + TLS termination
58.videoSearchQuery: load balancer vs api gateway difference
58.followUps: What is the difference between L4 and L7 load balancing? | What is sticky session and when do you need it? | How does a gateway protect downstream services from spikes? | What is the BFF (Backend-For-Frontend) pattern?
58.antiPatterns: Doing auth in every service instead of once at the gateway | Heavy business logic in the gateway — turns it into a single point of failure / scaling bottleneck | Using a single gateway for everything when BFF would be cleaner | No timeouts at the gateway — slow backend takes the whole gateway down

59.title: Find duplicates in an array
59.answer:
Naive: nested loop — O(n²).
Better: sort + adjacent check — O(n log n), O(1) extra space.
Optimal: HashSet pass — O(n) time, O(n) space.

Use HashSet unless you've been told to use no extra memory.
59.keyPoints: Time O(n) vs O(n²) | Space O(n) vs O(1) | HashSet.Add returns false on duplicate | LINQ GroupBy is short but slower for the simple ask
59.videoSearchQuery: find duplicates in array c# interview
59.followUps: What if the array has 100 million entries and doesn't fit in memory? | Find the duplicate without using extra memory — possible if 1..n with one duplicate (Floyd's algorithm). | Return the FIRST duplicate by occurrence — how does that change the code? | Return COUNT of each duplicate.
59.antiPatterns: Nested for-loop on large input | Calling .Contains() on a List in a loop — O(n²) | Sorting the input when you only need to detect duplicates (mutates caller's array)

60.title: Reverse a linked list
60.answer:
Iterative: walk with 3 pointers (prev, curr, next). Flip curr.next = prev each step. O(n) time, O(1) space.
Recursive: reverse the tail, then point head→tail. O(n) time, O(n) stack space.

Iterative is preferred — same time, better space.
60.keyPoints: 3-pointer technique | O(n) time, O(1) space iterative | Beware recursion depth on huge lists | Practise drawing it on paper before coding
60.followUps: Reverse only nodes between positions m and n. | Reverse in groups of k. | Detect if a linked list has a cycle (Floyd's tortoise & hare). | Find the middle of a linked list in one pass.
60.antiPatterns: Forgetting to set the old head's Next to null (creates a cycle) | Using a List<T> to collect and rebuild — defeats the point | Recursing on huge lists — StackOverflow

61.title: Two Sum — find pair with target sum
61.answer:
Brute force: try every pair. O(n²).
Optimal: one-pass HashMap — for each x, check if (target - x) was seen. O(n) time, O(n) space.

The key trick: as you iterate, the map contains all NUMBERS YOU'VE PASSED, mapped to their indices.
61.keyPoints: HashMap = value → index | One pass, not two | If target-x is in map, we have the answer | Works on sorted OR unsorted input
61.followUps: What if there are multiple valid pairs? Return all of them. | What if you need a TRIPLET that sums to target (3-Sum)? | What if the array is sorted — can you do O(1) extra space? | What if the array is huge and streamed?
61.antiPatterns: Nested for-loop — O(n²), gets timeout on LeetCode | Sorting first (loses original indices) | Using List<int>.IndexOf inside the loop — O(n²) hidden

62.title: Check if two strings are anagrams
62.answer:
Two strings are anagrams if they contain the SAME letters with the SAME frequency.

Approaches:
• Sort both, compare — O(n log n).
• Count letters (Dictionary or int[26]) — O(n) time, O(1) extra space if ASCII.

Count-array is the standard answer for interviews.
62.keyPoints: Same length required | Count, not sort | Watch case + spaces — normalize first | Unicode: use Dictionary, not int[26]
62.followUps: Make it case-insensitive AND ignore spaces. | Handle Unicode (emojis, accented characters). | Find the smallest window in s that is an anagram of t. | Count how many anagrams of t are in s.
62.antiPatterns: Sorting both strings via new string(arr.OrderBy()) when O(n) is asked | Counting one string, then the other — needs only ONE pass with +1/-1 | Forgetting to lowercase + trim

63.title: Fibonacci with memoization (DP)
63.answer:
Naive recursion is O(2ⁿ) — recomputes the same subproblems exponentially many times.

Two fixes:
• Top-down: recursion + memo table → O(n) time, O(n) space.
• Bottom-up: build up from 0 → O(n) time, O(1) space (just two variables).

Bottom-up is the canonical answer — fastest and cleanest.
63.keyPoints: Memoization = trade space for time | Bottom-up beats top-down for simple recurrences | Watch for integer overflow (use long / BigInteger past F(46)) | Pattern shows up in stair-climb, decode-ways, etc.
63.followUps: Climbing stairs (1 or 2 steps) — same recurrence. | House Robber — DP with constraint. | Decode Ways — DP with character look-ahead. | Why doesn't memoization help if subproblems are unique?
63.antiPatterns: Plain recursion without memo for n > 35 — seconds of CPU | Using Math.pow with Binet's formula — precision loss for large n | Storing the entire DP array when you only need the last 2 values

64.title: Binary Search
64.answer:
Works on a SORTED array. Repeatedly halves the search space.

O(log n) time — for 1 billion items you need ~30 comparisons.

Two common pitfalls: off-by-one on `mid` calculation, infinite loops with `l <= r` vs `l < r`.
64.keyPoints: Array MUST be sorted | mid = l + (r-l)/2 prevents overflow | l <= r with mid+1 / mid-1 is the simplest correct template | Variants: first occurrence, last occurrence, smallest >= target
64.followUps: Find FIRST occurrence of a duplicate value. | Search in a rotated sorted array. | Find the peak element (binary search by slope). | Bisect / lower_bound / upper_bound — what's each used for?
64.antiPatterns: Computing mid = (l+r)/2 in languages with integer overflow | l<r with mid update of `r = mid - 1` — skips potential answer | Re-implementing when Array.BinarySearch / List.BinarySearch exists in the stdlib

65.title: Detect a cycle in a linked list (Floyd's)
65.answer:
Use two pointers — slow (1 step) and fast (2 steps). If there is a cycle, fast catches up to slow inside the loop. If there isn't, fast reaches null.

Time O(n), space O(1) — no hash set needed.
65.keyPoints: Two pointers — tortoise & hare | Slow moves 1, fast moves 2 | If they meet → cycle exists | To find the START of the cycle: reset slow to head, advance both by 1 — they meet at the start
65.followUps: Why does fast=2*slow detect cycle? Prove it. | What's the length of the cycle? | Why does resetting slow to head and walking both by 1 find the start? | What if the cycle is exactly 1 node?
65.antiPatterns: Using a HashSet of visited nodes — works but O(n) extra space | Checking fast != slow before moving — off-by-one bug | Forgetting null checks on fast.Next

66.title: Longest substring without repeating characters
66.answer:
Classic sliding-window problem. Maintain a window [l, r] of characters, all unique.

• Expand r each step.
• If s[r] is already in the window, shrink l until it isn't.
• Track max length.

O(n) time, O(min(n, alphabet)) space.
66.keyPoints: Sliding window — left + right pointers | Dictionary of last-seen index speeds up the shrink | Window invariant: all chars in [l, r] are distinct
66.videoSearchQuery: longest substring without repeating characters sliding window
66.followUps: Generalize to longest substring with at most K distinct characters. | Longest substring with exactly K distinct. | What if the string is Unicode? | What if you also need to count how many such substrings of max length exist?
66.antiPatterns: Resetting the window from scratch on every conflict (back to O(n²)) | Using includes() in a loop (O(n) inside O(n)) | Forgetting to compare lastSeen index with current `l` — wrong shrink

67.title: What is Docker and what problem does it solve?
67.answer:
Docker packages an app + its dependencies + runtime + OS libs into a single image. The image runs identically on any host with Docker — your laptop, CI server, prod.

Solves "works on my machine" forever. Lightweight (shared kernel, no VM) — boots in seconds, runs hundreds per host.
67.keyPoints: Image = blueprint, Container = running instance | Dockerfile builds the image | Layered filesystem (each instruction = a layer) | Containers share host kernel — much lighter than VMs
67.codeSnippet:
# Multi-stage Dockerfile for an ASP.NET Core API

WORKDIR /src
COPY *.csproj ./
RUN dotnet restore
COPY . .
RUN dotnet publish -c Release -o /app

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:9.0
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app .
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["dotnet", "InterviewPrep.API.dll"]
67.commonUsage:
# Daily commands
docker build -t my-api .
docker run -p 8080:8080 my-api
docker ps                 # list running
docker logs <id>          # see logs
docker exec -it <id> bash # shell into
docker compose up -d      # whole stack from compose.yml
67.followUps: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT? | What is a multi-stage build and why use one? | How do you make images smaller? | What is the difference between a volume and a bind mount?
67.antiPatterns: Running as root inside the container | One image with build SDK still inside (huge image) | latest tag in prod (untraceable) | Storing secrets in the image — use env vars or secret manager

68.title: Docker vs Kubernetes — what's the difference?
68.answer:
Docker = how to PACKAGE & RUN a container on one host.
Kubernetes = how to ORCHESTRATE many containers across many hosts.

Think: Docker is the engine, Kubernetes is the air traffic control. You can run Docker without K8s. You cannot run K8s without container runtime (often containerd today, was Docker).
68.keyPoints: Docker → single-host packaging | K8s → multi-host orchestration | K8s gives self-healing, scaling, rolling deploys, service discovery, secrets | Use Docker for dev / single-server, K8s for prod-scale fleets

69.title: What is CI/CD? Explain a typical pipeline.
69.answer:
CI (Continuous Integration) = every push gets automatically built and tested.
CD (Continuous Delivery / Deployment) = if green, the artifact is deployed automatically to staging (Delivery) or prod (Deployment).

Why: catch regressions in minutes, not in QA two weeks later. Ship 10× a day instead of monthly.
69.keyPoints: Push → Build → Test → Package → Deploy | Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Azure DevOps, Jenkins | Run unit tests + integration + lint + security scan | Roll back automatically on health-check failure
69.codeSnippet:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: build
on: { push: { branches: [main] }, pull_request: {} }

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: 9.0 }
      - run: dotnet restore
      - run: dotnet build --no-restore -c Release
      - run: dotnet test --no-build -c Release --logger trx
      - name: Docker build & push
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        run: |
          docker build -t myregistry/api:${{ github.sha }} .
          docker push myregistry/api:${{ github.sha }}

70.title: Essential Git commands every developer must know
70.answer:
Git is the version control fabric of modern dev. Beyond add/commit/push, the senior-level commands are: rebase, cherry-pick, stash, reflog, bisect.

The mental model: Git tracks SNAPSHOTS, not diffs. Each commit is a tree. Branches are just pointers.
70.keyPoints: HEAD = current commit | Branches = movable pointers | Merge keeps history, rebase rewrites it | reflog saves you from EVERY 'I lost my work' situation | Push --force-with-lease, NEVER --force
70.codeSnippet:

git status                       # see what's going on
git add -p                       # stage changes interactively (great habit)
git commit -m "feat: add login"
git pull --rebase                # cleaner than --merge
git push origin feature/login

# Branching
git checkout -b feature/x

# Undo / recovery
git reset --soft HEAD~1          # undo last commit, keep changes staged
git reset --hard HEAD            # NUKE local changes (careful!)
git reflog                       # 'I lost a commit' — find it here
git stash / git stash pop        # park changes temporarily

# Inspecting
git log --oneline --graph --all
git diff main..feature/login
git blame path/to/file

# Finding bad commits

git bisect good v1.2.0
# git will check out commits in the middle — test, then say good/bad

72.title: What is Infrastructure as Code (Terraform / Bicep)?
72.answer:
IaC = define cloud infrastructure in CODE (text files), checked into git, applied automatically. Not via the AWS / Azure portal clicking buttons.

Why: reproducibility (recreate prod in 20 min), peer review (PR for infra changes), drift detection (state matches reality), disaster recovery.

Tools: Terraform (cloud-agnostic), AWS CloudFormation / CDK, Azure Bicep / ARM, Pulumi.
72.keyPoints: Declarative, not imperative | Plan → Apply | State file tracks reality | Modules = reusable building blocks | Environments = workspaces or separate state files

73.title: What is the Saga pattern?
73.answer:
Across services, you can't do an ACID transaction (no shared DB). The Saga pattern coordinates a multi-service business transaction as a SEQUENCE of local transactions, each with a COMPENSATING action if a later step fails.

Two flavors:
• ORCHESTRATION — a central coordinator drives each step (easier to reason about, single failure point).
• CHOREOGRAPHY — each service listens for events and decides what to do next (decoupled, harder to debug).

Classic example — book trip:
  1. ReserveFlight → ok
  2. ReserveHotel → ok
  3. ChargeCard → FAILS
  → CancelHotel + CancelFlight (compensating actions)
73.keyPoints: No 2PC across services | Each step is a LOCAL transaction | Failure → compensate, don't roll back | Orchestration is easier to start with | Idempotency is non-negotiable
73.followUps: What is the difference between Orchestration and Choreography saga? | What's an outbox pattern and why does saga need it? | How do you make compensating actions idempotent? | What if a compensating action itself fails?
73.antiPatterns: Distributed transaction across services (2PC) — XA over HTTP doesn't exist | Forgetting idempotency keys — duplicate messages → double charges | No timeout on the saga — stuck in 'processing' forever | Skipping a state log — impossible to debug

74.title: What is the Outbox Pattern?
74.answer:
Problem: in a service, you update your DB AND publish an event to Kafka / RabbitMQ. If you do them in separate steps and the broker is down, you have inconsistency:
  • Wrote DB but didn't publish → other services never hear about it.
  • Published but DB rollback → other services act on something that didn't happen.

Solution: write the event into an OUTBOX table inside the SAME DB transaction as the business change. A separate background worker reads from the outbox table and publishes to the broker. If the broker is down, the worker just retries — the DB is consistent.
74.keyPoints: DB + event in the SAME local transaction | Background relay publishes from outbox | At-least-once delivery — consumers must be idempotent | Variants: polling, CDC (Debezium), DB triggers
74.followUps: What's CDC (Change Data Capture) and how does Debezium use it for outbox? | What is the Inbox pattern? | Why must consumers be idempotent? | How do you clean up old outbox rows?
74.antiPatterns: Publishing event BEFORE saving DB (DB rollback → ghost event) | Publishing AFTER save without outbox (broker down → lost event) | Consumers without idempotency keys → double-charge / double-ship | Letting outbox table grow forever — needs cleanup job

75.title: Idempotency in distributed systems
75.answer:
An operation is IDEMPOTENT if calling it twice with the same input has the SAME effect as calling it once.

Why it matters: any network call can be retried (timeout, broker redelivery, user double-click). Without idempotency you get duplicate orders, double charges, double emails.

How:
1. Client sends an Idempotency-Key header (UUID).
2. Server stores the result of each key for some hours.
3. Same key arrives again → return the SAVED result, don't re-execute.
75.keyPoints: Same input → same effect, no matter how many calls | GET / PUT / DELETE are idempotent by definition. POST is not. | Idempotency-Key header + server-side dedup table | Critical for payments, order placement, sending emails
75.followUps: Why are GET requests considered idempotent? | What's the difference between idempotent and safe? | How long should you keep idempotency keys? | What if the same key arrives with a DIFFERENT body?
75.antiPatterns: Treating POST as idempotent without a key — every retry creates a new row | Generating a new key on every retry — kills the point | Storing keys forever — table explosion | Returning a different response for the same key — silent inconsistency

76.title: Circuit Breaker pattern
76.answer:
A downstream service is failing — every request hangs for 30s then fails. Without protection, your service hangs too, consumes threads, then YOU fail. Cascade.

The Circuit Breaker watches failures. Above a threshold, it OPENS — for some cool-off period, calls fail FAST without even trying. After the cool-off, it goes HALF-OPEN — lets a few test calls through. If they succeed, CLOSE again. If they fail, OPEN for another cool-off.

Three states: CLOSED (normal) → OPEN (fail fast) → HALF-OPEN (testing) → back to CLOSED or OPEN.
76.keyPoints: Prevents cascading failures | Three states: Closed / Open / Half-Open | Pair with timeout + retry + bulkhead | .NET: Polly / Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience | Java: Resilience4j
76.followUps: How is Circuit Breaker different from Retry? | What is a bulkhead and why combine with circuit breaker? | How do you choose threshold and cool-off values? | What is graceful degradation?
76.antiPatterns: Retry without circuit breaker — multiplies load on the failing service | One breaker for all endpoints — one slow endpoint trips the whole thing | Cool-off too short — keeps slamming a broken service | No fallback — circuit opens, request fails, user sees a 500. Provide a cached / degraded response when possible.

77.title: BFF — Backend For Frontend pattern
77.answer:
One generic API for web + mobile + desktop ends up serving the LOWEST common denominator — too many round trips for one client, too much data for another.

BFF = each frontend (web / mobile / desktop) gets its OWN backend, tailored to its needs. Each BFF aggregates calls to the underlying microservices, shapes the response for its specific client, and handles its own auth flow.

The web BFF can batch 3 calls into 1; the mobile BFF can return only the fields a phone needs.
77.keyPoints: One BFF per consumer (web, mobile, desktop) | BFF owned by the FRONTEND team | Reduces over-fetching / under-fetching | Often becomes the GraphQL layer | Don't put business logic in the BFF — only orchestration / shaping
77.followUps: How is BFF different from an API gateway? | When is a BFF overkill? | What's the relationship between BFF and GraphQL? | Where does authentication live in a BFF setup?
77.antiPatterns: One BFF used by every client (it's just an API gateway then) | Business logic creeping into the BFF — should stay in domain services | BFF making N sequential calls instead of parallel | No timeouts on downstream calls — one slow service stalls the whole BFF response

78.title: Distributed tracing — what is it and why?
78.answer:
One user request hits 8 microservices behind the scenes. When something is slow / broken, you have NO idea which hop is the bottleneck — each service has its own logs.

Distributed tracing solves this. Every request gets a TRACE ID. As it hops between services, each hop adds a SPAN (a timed slice) under that trace. A UI (Jaeger / Tempo / Zipkin) shows the full waterfall — exactly where the time went.

.NET has built-in System.Diagnostics.Activity that follows the OpenTelemetry spec. Modern dotnet exports to OTEL collectors out of the box.
78.keyPoints: Trace = entire user request | Span = one operation within it | Trace ID propagated across HTTP / messaging | OpenTelemetry = vendor-neutral standard | Jaeger / Tempo / Zipkin = backends
78.followUps: What's the difference between metrics, logs, and traces? | What is the W3C Trace Context header? | How do you propagate trace context across message queues? | What is sampling and why is it needed at scale?
78.antiPatterns: Logging trace ID is enough — no, you also need the waterfall view | Sampling all traces in prod — explodes storage; sample 1-10% in high-throughput services | Trace context dropped at the message queue boundary | Spans without tags — you have a timeline but no business context

81.title: Resume rules that actually move recruiters
81.answer:
Recruiters scan a resume for 6-10 seconds. ATS (Applicant Tracking Systems) parse it before a human ever sees it. Optimize for both.

1. ONE page (until you have 8+ years).
2. No fancy templates — single column, standard fonts. ATS gets confused by 2-column / icons / tables.
3. Top: name, role, contact, GitHub, LinkedIn, portfolio.
4. Skills section — TECHNOLOGIES ONLY (C#, .NET 8, EF Core, Angular, SQL Server, Azure). The system filters on these keywords.
5. Experience bullets follow XYZ: "Accomplished X (number) by Y (action) which led to Z (impact)".
6. Include the EXACT keywords from the job description you're applying for.

KILL: photo, age, marital status, hobbies, MS Word default skill bars, generic 'team player' lines.

82.title: How to write a cover letter that actually gets read
82.answer:
90% of cover letters say the same thing — "I'm passionate about technology, I'm a team player, please consider me." That's why they get skimmed in 5 seconds.

FORMULA THAT WORKS — 4 short paragraphs:
1. WHY THEM (1-2 lines) — name one specific thing about the company / role that pulled you. ("I noticed your engineering blog post on switching from RabbitMQ to Kafka — that's exactly the kind of migration I led at...")
2. WHY YOU (2-3 lines) — pick ONE accomplishment that maps to the JD. Numbers.
3. WHY NOW (1-2 lines) — what you're looking for next, framed as growth, not escape.
4. CTA — "Happy to walk through any of this in a call."

Keep it under 250 words. No 'I look forward to hearing from you.'

84.title: How to ace the on-site / final round
84.answer:
On-site (or its remote equivalent) is 3-6 hours: coding, system design, behavioral, lunch with team, sometimes a live debugging or architecture deep-dive.

MENTAL FRAME — they've ALREADY decided you can probably do the job. On-site is about: would I want to work with this person? Can they think out loud? Are they good in a room?

MECHANICAL TIPS:
1. Eat properly before. Hydrate. Bring water.
2. Think OUT LOUD on every problem — your reasoning matters more than the answer.
3. Ask CLARIFYING questions before coding. Always.
4. If stuck, say 'Let me think about a simpler version first' — never silence.
5. At lunch, you're STILL being interviewed. Stay engaged but relax.
6. After every round, write 2 lines of notes for your follow-up email.
7. Send a thank-you email same-day. Reference one specific thing.

85.title: HTTP status codes — the ones you must know
85.answer:
Memorize the BUCKETS first, then the specific codes:

**1xx** — Informational (rarely seen in app code)
**2xx** — Success
**3xx** — Redirect
**4xx** — Client error (you, the caller, did something wrong)
**5xx** — Server error (the API broke)

201 Created           — POST created a resource (also include Location header)

88.title: Linux signals & process control
88.answer: Signals are how Unix sends messages to processes. Knowing the common ones (and how to handle them) matters for graceful shutdown, container lifecycle, and debugging.
88.keyPoints: SIGTERM (15) — polite stop, app should clean up | SIGKILL (9) — instant death, can't be caught | SIGINT (2) — Ctrl+C | SIGHUP (1) — reload config | SIGSTOP / SIGCONT — pause/resume

# SIGUSR1   10   custom — apps use it for things like log rotation

90.title: Git aliases that make you 3× faster
90.answer:
Drop these into `~/.gitconfig`. After one week you'll wonder how you lived without them.

The big wins: `git st`, `git lg` (pretty log), `git undo` (uncommit but keep changes), `git wip` (quick wip commit), `git unwip`.
90.keyPoints: Set once in ~/.gitconfig | st = status, ci = commit, co = checkout | lg = pretty graph log | undo = soft reset HEAD~1 | wip / unwip for quick parking
90.codeSnippet:
# Open ~/.gitconfig and add:

[alias]
  st       = status -sb
  co       = checkout
  br       = branch
  ci       = commit
  ca       = commit --amend --no-edit
  cm       = commit -m
  unstage  = reset HEAD --
  last     = log -1 HEAD
  undo     = reset --soft HEAD~1

  # pretty log graph — the GOAT
  lg       = log --graph --abbrev-commit --decorate \
             --format=format:'%C(yellow)%h%C(reset) %C(white)%s%C(reset) \
             %C(dim white)- %an%C(reset)%C(auto)%d%C(reset)' --all

  # quick WIP — park your work
  wip      = !git add -A && git commit -m '--wip-- [skip ci]'
  unwip    = reset HEAD~1

  # what branches have I been on lately?
  recent   = !git for-each-ref --sort=-committerdate refs/heads/ \
             --format='%(committerdate:relative)%09%(refname:short)' \
             | head -10

  # interactive cleanup
  cleanup  = !git branch --merged | grep -v '\\*' | grep -v main \
             | grep -v master | xargs -n 1 git branch -d
90.commonUsage:

git lg                    # gorgeous log graph
git cm "feat: add login"  # commit
git ca                    # amend last (no edit)
git undo                  # "undo last commit, keep my changes staged"
git wip                   # park everything as WIP
git unwip                 # ...bring it back
git recent                # last 10 branches you worked on
git cleanup               # delete already-merged branches
